scenes.tts: By the 1950s the lock-and-key picture decorated every textbook, and Daniel Koshland knew it was incomplete — because of water.

scenes.tts: If an active site sat permanently open and waiting, water, smaller than any substrate, should slip in constantly and trigger chaos. It doesn't.
scenes.visual: permanently open site; water slips in, chaos; it doesn't
scenes.narration: If an active site sat permanently open and waiting, water, smaller than any substrate, should slip in constantly and trigger chaos. It doesn't.

scenes.tts: So something must change when the real substrate arrives: the site closes around it, and the complementarity that matters is reached not at the resting substrate but at the strained transition state. Binding induces the fit, and water is too small to force it.
scenes.visual: site closes on real substrate; grip tightest at strained transition state; binding induces fit; water too small to force it

scenes.tts: The idea cut so hard against the dogma that the standard journals turned it away; one reviewer's verdict became famous ("What is new is not true, and what is true is not new").
scenes.narration: The idea cut so hard against the dogma that the standard journals turned it away; one reviewer's verdict became famous ("What is new is not true, and what is true is not new").

scenes.tts: Koshland slipped the paper into PNAS in 1958 through a loophole, and X-ray crystallography later proved him right: enzymes flex, shift, and clamp down. He had moved biochemistry from a science of static shapes to one of moving machines.
